D018-D020_h001.question:
I’ve been having these dreams—same one lately, mostly—where I’m back at the register and the guy pulls the gun out, but this time I can’t move, can’t say anything, just frozen while everything goes dark. I wake up sweating, heart slamming like I just ran a mile. It takes forever to calm down, sometimes I’m still shaky hours later. 

Work’s been… hard. I used to just show up, clock in, do the job. Now I drag myself there. Some days I can’t even decide what to wear, stand there staring at my clothes like it’s a huge choice. Feels like nothing matters, but I don’t know why I care so much about that night, why it sticks. 

I keep thinking—if the guy at the counter hadn’t delayed me, asking for lotto tickets right before, maybe I wouldn’t’ve been there when the guy came in. I know it’s not his fault, not really, but it’s easier to be mad at him than… than at myself for freezing. Feels like I should’ve done something. Now I feel stupid, weak, like I let myself down. 

It’s only been a few weeks, I guess. I didn’t think I’d still feel this raw. Some days I’m okay. Others, I just can’t face it.
D018-D020_h001.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h001.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h002.question: I’ve been having these dreams—over and over—where I’m back in that moment, reliving everything. It’s not just fragments; I feel it all: the panic, the sounds, even the smell. I wake up shaky, sometimes crying, and it takes forever to calm down. Since it happened, I’ve been pulling away from people. I love my husband, but I don’t know… I don’t feel like talking much, even to him. We used to go out with friends all the time, but now I make excuses. I just feel safer at home. I keep thinking it was my fault—like I should’ve seen it coming or reacted differently. That thought won’t leave me alone. I’m constantly on edge, like something bad’s about to happen. Even little things—a door slamming, a phone buzzing—make me jump. I flinch, sometimes even drop things. Deciding what to wear in the morning feels impossible. I stand there frozen, like every choice has huge consequences. I want to feel normal again, but I don’t even know when this started to feel so heavy. It’s been weeks… or maybe a little more? Time feels blurry.
D018-D020_h002.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h002.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h003.question:
I’ve been having a hard time since the accident—three weeks now. It wasn’t just a fender-bender; a pedestrian was involved, and even though it wasn’t my fault—weather, poor visibility—I keep replaying it. Sometimes, when someone walks too close behind me at the lab or when a monitor flickers like headlights, my chest tightens and I feel dizzy, like I can’t breathe. I’ve always loved my work—solving puzzles in genomic data—but now nothing feels rewarding. I sit at my desk and stare at the screen. Even dinner with my husband, which used to be something I looked forward to, just feels… flat.

I know I shouldn’t, but I keep thinking about the other driver who swerved into my lane before it happened. I keep wondering why he didn’t slow down, why he wasn’t more careful—like he should’ve protected me somehow. And then I hate myself for it, because someone got hurt, and I survived. I lie awake most nights with that guilt. 

Even picking what to wear in the morning feels overwhelming. I stand there, paralyzed. And if someone walks into my home office quickly, even my husband, I flinch like I’ve been hit. I don’t know if this is normal or if I’m falling apart. I can’t tell if it’s too soon to judge.
D018-D020_h003.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h003.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h004.question:
I’ve been having a hard time since… well, since that day at the grocery store when the robbery happened. I can’t get it out of my head—the shouting, the gun, people screaming. It just pops up when I’m sitting quietly, even when I’m trying to relax. My wife says I flinch if she touches my shoulder without warning, which I never used to do.  

I don’t go out much anymore, even to the coffee shop where I used to meet my old colleagues. It’s not that I don’t want to see them, exactly—it just feels like too much effort. I keep thinking they wouldn’t understand anyway. I find myself getting angry, too—like the cashier moved too slow, or the neighbor parks too close to my gate. I know it sounds petty, but it builds up inside, and sometimes I snap.  

I blame the store manager, really. He should’ve had security after what happened last year. If he’d done something then, this wouldn’t have happened.  

Even little things—what to eat, what shirt to wear—take forever to decide. I stand there, frozen, like it’s some big life choice.  

It’s only been… a few weeks, I think. I can’t say whether it’s getting better or worse. Some days I feel like I’m overreacting; others, I don’t know how to stop.
D018-D020_h004.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h004.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h005.question:
I’ve been struggling since that incident at school last month—when the lockdown happened. I keep seeing it again in my head, like it’s playing on a loop: the sirens, the students huddled in corners, not knowing if someone was coming. It just pops up, even when I’m trying to relax. Ever since, I haven’t touched my guitar. I used to play every evening. Now I just feel… hollow. I can’t get into anything. 

I’ve also been on edge. If someone touches my shoulder unexpectedly, I jump like I’ve been shocked. It’s embarrassing—especially in staff meetings. I can’t keep up with conversations anymore; my mind drifts, and I have to ask people to repeat themselves. I feel tense all the time, like something’s about to happen. 

I know logically the danger’s passed, but I can’t shake the fear. And honestly? I keep thinking about how certain staff didn’t follow protocol. If they’d acted faster, maybe none of it would’ve felt so out of control. I know it might not be fair, but I can’t stop replaying it—their hesitation, the chaos. It’s been weeks, but I don’t know if I’m getting better or just holding on.
D018-D020_h005.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h005.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h006.question:
I’ve been off ever since that accident with the tractor last month—well, part of it, anyway. I remember the noise, the smell of diesel… but after that, everything’s spotty. Can’t piece together how I got out. Some mornings, I wake up with my heart jackhammering, like it’s happening all over again. Little things set me off—my wife touched my shoulder the other day, and I damn near knocked her back. Felt bad after, but it’s like my body reacts before my mind catches up.  

I don’t talk about it much. In fact, I try not to think about it at all. If the boys bring it up at the feed store, I change the subject or walk off. Feels easier that way. Truth is, some days I don’t feel much of anything—just hollow. My wife says I’m distant, like I’m not really there. I love her, I do, but I can’t always show it.  

The anger… that’s new. Snapped at one of the hands over a misplaced tool. Wasn’t his fault. It’s like something’s just beneath the skin, restless. But I don’t know if this is all still the shock wearing off, or something more. Hard to say what’s normal after something like this.
D018-D020_h006.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h006.answer: A & B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h007.question:
I’ve been having these flashes—pictures in my head that just show up, like the accident scene, fragments of the ambulance, the sound of glass. I can’t control when they come. Sometimes I’m at work, writing scripts, and suddenly I’m back there, heart racing. It’s been weeks, but I don’t know if it’s getting better. I avoid my usual coffee shop—the one near the intersection where it happened. I even cut off a friend who wanted to meet there. Honestly, I’ve pulled back from a lot of things.

I remember pieces of that night—like the streetlight flickering—but whole stretches are just gone. How I got into the car, what I said right after… blank. The weirdest part? I hugged my sister last week and felt nothing. No warmth, no connection. It scared me. I used to fall in love easily; now even the idea feels distant, like a habit I forgot how to do.

And if someone touches me without warning—like a hand on my shoulder—I jump. Once, I yelled at a colleague who startled me, started swearing. I felt awful, but it just burst out. I don’t want to be like this, but I can’t tell if it’s grief, shock, or something bigger. It hasn’t been a month yet, really. I just don’t know what’s normal.
D018-D020_h007.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h007.answer: A & B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h008.question:
I’ve been having these flashes—moments when I’m right back there, seeing things I can’t explain, like images just force their way into my head. I don’t know why they come, and I can’t stop them. Sometimes I’ll hear a siren or a car backfire and I jump, my whole body tenses like I’m under attack. I’ve broken a few things—mugs, a lamp—just out of nowhere, lashing out when someone startles me.  

I don’t go out much anymore. Not since the divorce. I avoid certain streets, certain sounds... conversations that might lead somewhere deep. I don’t like talking about the past—it feels like there’s a gap in my memory, like whole pieces are just gone. I can’t even tell you what happened during that time. It’s blank.  

I used to feel close to people. Now, it’s like I’m watching love from behind glass. My sister calls, and I know I should feel something, but I don't. My ex used to say I was warm. Now? I don’t know who I am.  

It’s only been a few weeks since things got like this—hard to tell, really. Time’s been strange. I just write now, all night, for other people’s lives. Mine feels like it’s on pause.
D018-D020_h008.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h008.answer: A & B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h009.question:
I’ve been feeling… off… for a few weeks now—ever since that night. I don’t talk about it, and I’ve stopped going to that part of town. Even the scent of rain on pavement brings this wave of dread, like my body remembers before my mind does. Sometimes I’ll be cueing breath in a class, and suddenly I’m *back there*—heart racing, tasting copper, certain the room is collapsing. It only lasts a few seconds, but I lose track. My students notice.  

I remember pieces—the broken taillight, the voice shouting—but not how I got out of the car. That frustrates me. I used to light up teaching restorative poses, now I just go through the motions. A student told me I smiled for the first time in months last week when her mom brought cookies. I didn’t even feel it.  

My roommate hugged me from behind the other day and I screamed—knocked over a lamp. I didn’t recognize her. And yeah, I’ve snapped. Told a client to “just leave” when she asked why I was spacing out. I hate that. I’m supposed to be the calm one.  

I don’t know if this is just grief, or shock, or what. It’s not like I can’t function, but… something’s broken.
D018-D020_h009.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h009.answer: A & B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h010.question:
I’ve been off since it happened—maybe a few weeks? It’s hard to keep track. Sometimes I hear a loud bang in the kitchen, like a pot dropping, and I flinch so hard I drop whatever I’m holding. My hands shake. It’s embarrassing in class. I don’t go near the dishwashing area anymore; the clatter, the sudden sounds—it just gets to me. I’ve stopped eating at the cafeteria too. Something about the noise feels… unsafe.

There are gaps in what I remember. Whole pieces of that night are just gone. I know I made it home, but I don’t know how. People ask, and I can’t tell them. I don’t want to talk about it. I avoid the streets near where it happened. I even changed my route to school.

I got praised last week for my plating—finally got that technique right—but I didn’t feel anything. Just numb. My instructor said I should be proud, but pride feels like a foreign language.

I’m short-tempered lately. Little things—a delayed bus, someone bumping into me—set me off. I didn’t used to be like this. I just want to get back to cooking, but it’s like I’m moving through fog. I don’t know if I’m healing or stuck.
D018-D020_h010.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h010.answer: A & B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h011.question:
I’ve been struggling since that case last month—the one where the little boy was found in the garage, malnourished and scared. I keep replaying the moment I opened that door. Even hearing a garage door close at my own house makes my chest tighten, my hands sweat. I try not to think about it, but it creeps in when I’m quiet—during my commute, in the shower. So I’ve started filling every silence with podcasts, music, anything to keep my mind off it.  

I keep thinking, *I should’ve seen the signs sooner. I’m supposed to protect kids like him, but I failed.* It’s like I’m broken somehow—like I don’t even trust myself anymore, not in my job, not at home. My husband says I’ve been quick to snap lately. Last week I yelled at him for leaving his shoes out, really tore into him, and I could see he was stunned. I didn’t mean to—those feelings just explode before I can catch them.  

I don’t know if it’s just been too much lately, or if I’m not cut out for this work anymore. Some days it feels like everything is piling up, and I don’t know how long I’ve felt this way—weeks, maybe? I can’t tell if it will pass or if it’s something… bigger.
D018-D020_h011.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h011.answer: D & A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h012.question:
I’ve been having a hard time since… well, since that incident last year. A client meeting went off the rails—security got involved, I was restrained, felt completely powerless. I don’t talk about it, not even with my ex-wife, though we still co-parent. Honestly, I avoid anything that reminds me of it—certain offices, high-pressure negotiations, even the train line I used to take downtown. Just seeing someone who looks like one of the security guards sets me on edge.  

I keep thinking, “You can’t trust anyone.” Clients, colleagues—anyone could turn in an instant. I blamed the firm’s legal team, really—why didn’t they intervene? They let it happen. Now I see danger everywhere, like people are just waiting to corner you.  

And my temper? It’s like a live wire. Small things—a delayed call, a misplaced file—send me into a rage. I know it’s not rational, but I can’t help it. I’ve been like this for… a while. I won’t say how long exactly, but it’s messing with my work, and I’m exhausted from holding it together.
D018-D020_h012.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h012.answer: D & A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h013.question:
I’ve been having these dreams—over and over—about the storm. Not just any storm, but *that* one. The night of the tornado outbreak last spring. I keep reliving it: the radar spinning out of control, the emergency broadcasts, the calls from people trapped in their homes. In the dream, I’m at the anchor desk, but no one hears me. I scream the warnings, but the audio’s cut. I wake up drenched, heart slamming, like I’ve lived it again.  

Since then, I can’t even look at the radar maps without feeling this tightness in my chest. I’ve stopped checking the overnight forecasts. My wife notices—I used to love that part. Now, I just shut down if it comes up. I keep thinking… maybe if I’d stressed it harder that night, pushed the tone more, someone might’ve listened. I feel like I’m cracked somehow—like I let everyone down. And my producer? He downplayed the risk during the live cut-in. I keep thinking it should’ve been *his* voice cracking, not mine.  

Lately, I’ve snapped at my team over small things—messed-up graphics, delays in the feed—just exploded. I didn’t used to be like this. It’s only been a few weeks, though. Maybe I just need time. Or maybe this is how it stays.
D018-D020_h013.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h013.answer: D & A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h014.question:
I’ve been having a hard time since that incident a few weeks ago—this security breach at the ministry, where I was nearly caught in the middle of it. Even now, if someone slams a door too loud, my chest tightens and I feel like I can’t breathe. I’ve started taking different routes to work, avoiding the wing where it happened. I don’t want to think about it, honestly. The memories just come anyway—flashbacks, almost—and they leave me shaky.  

I keep telling myself that if someone had just followed protocol, none of this would’ve happened. A colleague in communications—I know it’s not fair, maybe, but I can’t help thinking they downplayed the threat. Now I wonder if anyone actually takes security seriously. Trusting people feels impossible. I snap at my team during briefings—last week I yelled when someone made a small error. I regret it after, but in the moment, I just feel like everything’s spinning.  

It’s been difficult to focus, to sleep. Some days I feel like I’m overreacting. Other days, it feels like it just happened. I haven’t missed work, but I’m not myself. I don’t know if this is supposed to last this long.
D018-D020_h014.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h014.answer: D & A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h015.question:
I’ve been struggling since the campus lockdown last month—when that active shooter alert went off. I was on duty, helping a family tour the building when everything shut down. We were stuck for hours. Ever since, I keep having these moments where I’m right back there—the sirens, the voices over the loudspeaker, my hands shaking as I tried to calm that student who was crying. It feels real, like I’m there again, and I don’t realize I’ve stopped talking or frozen up until my wife says something.

I avoid going near schools now—even our local community center. My wife teaches yoga there, and I used to meet her, but I can’t. Just driving past makes my chest tighten. I’ve snapped at coworkers over small things. Last week I threw a stack of files across my office. I don’t know why I’m like this. I should’ve done more—should’ve guided more families to safety. Now it feels like the world’s just waiting to collapse again. But honestly, I’m not sure how long this’s been going on. A few weeks? It’s all blurred together.
D018-D020_h015.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h015.answer: D & A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h016.question:
I’ve been having these intense dreams—reliving that night over and over, the sirens, the rain, the way everything felt out of control. It’s not just the images; it’s the fear that stays with me when I wake up, like I’m still trapped there. Since it happened, I avoid anything that brings it back—the subway station near where it occurred, late-night rides, even certain conversations with colleagues when they talk about commuting. It’s easier to just stay away.  

I can’t help but think it could’ve been prevented—if my manager hadn’t pushed us to stay so late, if security had been better. It’s not just bad luck; someone should’ve done more. I know that might sound harsh, but I keep replaying it, wondering who dropped the ball.  

At work, I’m constantly aware of my surroundings—the exits, who’s around, anything that feels off. It started right after, and it hasn’t really let up. I can’t say exactly how long it’s been—weeks, maybe? I haven’t been tracking, just trying to get through each day. Some mornings feel like I’m bracing for something, even when nothing’s happening.
D018-D020_h016.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h016.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h017.question:
I’ve been off since that incident at work last month—can’t really shake it. There’s this one spot near the loading dock where it happened, and I just can’t bring myself to go back there. I ask one of the younger staff to handle it now. Even walking past the hallway triggers something—my chest tightens, and my mind just races. I keep seeing that falling shelf in my head, like a loop.  

I blame myself, truthfully. I’ve worked that building for over twenty years. Should’ve noticed the way it was leaning. Could’ve said something. Now I second-guess everything. When I’m on shift, I’m always scanning—doors, exits, who’s coming in. I check the emergency routes more than I need to, I know. My wife says I’m jumpy, like I’m waiting for something bad to happen again.  

It’s not every second, but it’s there, humming in the background. Some days are okay. Others, I’m just… on edge. I haven’t missed work—at least I’ve held on to that—but I can’t say how much longer I’ll manage. I don’t know if this is just me struggling to get past it, or if it’s becoming something more.
D018-D020_h017.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h017.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h018.question:
I’ve been having a hard time since the bridge collapse last… well, it’s been a few weeks, I guess. I was on site the day it happened—right there when it went down. I keep seeing the images, even when I close my eyes. Loud noises, like metal clanging or a sudden horn, make my chest tighten. I had to ask my wife not to play the news in the living room anymore—she doesn’t understand, but I just can’t watch the footage.

I’ve stopped going near construction zones. I used to drive by just to observe, out of habit, but now I reroute, even if it takes longer. I don’t talk about the project with colleagues, not even at work meetings. It feels too raw.

I think about it constantly—what I could’ve caught in the review, whether I missed signs. I was the lead, after all. Should’ve caught something. My wife says it wasn’t me, but still… 

I’m always looking around now—checking exits, watching the road ahead, scanning the structure of buildings when I walk by. It’s like my mind won’t shut it off. I don’t know if this is normal or if I’m overreacting. Maybe it’ll pass. I just need to stay alert, just in case.
D018-D020_h018.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h018.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h019.question:
I’ve been having these awful dreams—reliving the accident, seeing the headlights, hearing the crash. It’s been happening almost every night since it happened. I wake up panicked, heart racing, drenched in sweat. During the day, I can’t stand being near intersections or even hearing screeching tires. I’ve started taking longer routes to work just to avoid that stretch of road. I don’t go near my car unless I absolutely have to, and I won’t talk about it—not with my friends, not with my assistant, nobody.  

I keep thinking it was my fault. I was tired that night. I knew I shouldn’t have driven, but I did anyway. If I’d just called a rideshare… I should’ve known better.  

I’m always on edge now. In meetings, I sit with my back to the wall so I can see the door. At home, I check the locks twice, three times—windows, doors, everything. I scan every room, every parking garage, looking for anything that feels “off.” It’s exhausting. I can’t focus on design details like I used to, and my team has noticed. But I can’t explain to them that I just feel like danger’s always close, just around the corner.  

It’s only been… a few weeks, I think? Time’s been blurry. I’m just trying to hold things together.
D018-D020_h019.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h019.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h020.question:
I’ve been struggling since the accident a few weeks ago—when my husband and I were hit head-on by a drunk driver. I wasn’t badly hurt physically, but something’s just off. Sometimes, even hearing a car door slam too hard makes my chest tighten and I’ll freeze for a second, like I’m right back there. I don’t like driving anymore. Even sitting in the passenger seat, if someone brakes suddenly, I can feel my heart racing, my hands go clammy. I try not to think about it—the moment of impact, what could’ve happened—but those thoughts just sneak in, especially at night. So I distract myself, scroll on my phone until I’m exhausted. 

At work, I keep noticing myself checking the exits, or flinching when a high-speed handpiece whirs loudly—it’s not the same, but something about the sharpness of it. I know it’s irrational, but I can’t help it. And I keep replaying it—thinking, *what if I had left five minutes earlier? What if I’d taken a different route?* It wasn’t my fault, logically I know that, but still. It’s hard not to feel like I should’ve stopped it somehow. I love my patients, but lately it’s been harder to focus, like my mind’s half elsewhere. I just don’t know how long I’ll feel like this.
D018-D020_h020.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h020.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h021.question:
I’ve been having these flashes—sudden memories that just crash into my head, like a piano key sticking and playing the same wrong note over and over. It’s always that moment, that one night, even though I don’t want to think about it. It just comes. Sometimes I’m teaching a student, and suddenly I’m back there, heart pounding, fingers freezing over the keys.  

I feel… detached. Like there’s a glass wall between me and everyone else. My husband tries to hold me, but I can’t sink into it like I used to. I love him, I know I do, but the warmth just doesn’t come. And underneath it all, there’s this constant shame, like I did something wrong, even though logically I know it wasn’t my fault.  

The worst part is how wound up I feel all the time. Little things—like a door slamming or a student missing a note—make me want to snap. I don’t yell, but I can feel the heat rise, like my nerves are bare wires. I don’t even know how long this has been going on—weeks, maybe? I lost track. It’s just… always there now, coloring everything.
D018-D020_h021.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h021.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h022.question:
I’ve been struggling since… well, since that incident at work a few weeks ago. I don’t even want to say what happened—it just makes my chest tighten. But ever since, if someone slams a door or raises their voice nearby, I freeze. My heart races, and I feel like I’m right back there. It’s like my body doesn’t know it’s over.

I keep thinking about how I reacted—I couldn’t move fast enough, and now I just feel… weak. Ashamed, I guess. Like I should’ve done something differently. Even when my husband tells me I did nothing wrong, it doesn’t really sink in. Last week I got praised at work for catching an error, but it felt hollow. I didn’t feel proud—just numb.

And my temper… it’s not like me. I snapped at my husband yesterday, yelling over nothing. Cursed and blamed him for being late, even though it wasn’t his fault. Afterward, I cried. I don’t recognize myself. I just feel raw all the time. I don’t know if it’ll fade or if this is how it’s going to be now. I can’t tell if I’m just adjusting… or stuck.
D018-D020_h022.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h022.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h023.question:
I’ve been struggling to sleep—night after night, I have these dreams about the accident. I’m back in the car, rain slamming the windshield, headlights coming straight at me… I wake up with my heart racing, sometimes in tears. It’s been happening for… I don’t know, a few weeks now? Maybe a bit more. I can’t even say for sure.  

Ever since it happened, I just feel… numb. I got recognized at the district meeting last week—awarded for improving graduation rates—but I didn’t feel proud. I just sat there, thinking about what I *didn’t* do, what I could’ve handled better. I keep replaying the crash, wondering why I survived when the other driver didn’t. I wasn’t even hurt badly, but… I can’t shake the guilt. Like I should’ve done something differently.  

And my patience? Gone. I snap at my staff over tiny things—a late form, a miscommunication. I don’t mean to, but everything feels like too much. My husband says I’m on edge all the time. I just want to feel like myself again, but I don’t even know when this started or how long it’ll last. Maybe it’ll fade. I keep hoping it will.
D018-D020_h023.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h023.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h024.question:
I’ve been having a really hard time since my car accident—maybe four or five weeks ago now. It wasn’t life-threatening, at least not physically, but something about it just got stuck in my head. I keep seeing flashes of the headlights, the sound of the horn blaring, and suddenly I’m back there, heart racing, palms sweating. Even driving past the intersection where it happened makes me feel like I can’t breathe.

I’m constantly on edge, like something bad is about to happen, even when I know logically I’m safe. At work, I snap at my nurse over the smallest things—a misplaced chart, a delayed patient—and then I feel awful afterward. My husband says I don’t laugh like I used to. We went out with friends last weekend, and everyone was having fun. I smiled, said all the right things, but inside, I was empty. Like joy is behind glass—visible, but untouchable.

I want to believe this is just me adjusting, that it’ll pass. But I’m starting to wonder if it’s more than that. I don’t know how long this is supposed to last. Part of me thinks I should be over it by now.
D018-D020_h024.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h024.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h025.question:
I’ve been having a hard time since that call last month—well, really a few calls piling up, but one in particular sticks. I keep seeing the kid’s backpack in my rearview, something about it just hits me wrong. Doesn’t make sense, but it’s like my chest gets tight and my jaw clenches. I don’t know, maybe it’s dumb. 

I’ve been angry a lot—really angry. Not even about the job stuff. My partner said I snapped at a guy for cutting me off in traffic, but it wasn’t just that. Feels like there’s a fire under my skin all the time. I can’t shut it off. And when I do try to cool down, it’s not like anything helps. Even when I got promoted last week—something I worked for—I didn’t feel anything. Just… flat. Like pride doesn’t live in me anymore.

I sleep light, if at all. Jump at noises. I yelled at a neighbor over their dog barking the other night. It wasn’t bad, but something just snapped. I don’t like how I’m acting. It’s not who I am—or who I used to be. But I can’t say exactly when it started, or if it’ll pass. Could be stress. Could be more. I just don’t know how long this’ll stick around.
D018-D020_h025.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h025.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder
